subject: Gateway fallback playbook: VPC Peering vs PrivateLink vs Site-to-Site VPN
messages:

Subject: Guidance request: connectivity options for our on-prem LLM pilot

Hi Kimberly,

Thanks again for taking the time earlier. EdgeGate is ready to spin up a small on-prem pilot of Redwood Private (single rack, strict egress policy). We have three constraints that are driving questions about connectivity:

- No routable public IPs on the application hosts (we NAT at border and have limited static IPs).
- We need source IP continuity for our audit/logging and per-tenant routing.
- Predictable latency to the Redwood control plane but also the option to fail over to a lower-cost path during capacity events.

Can you outline the operational tradeoffs between VPC Peering (or cloud-equivalent peering), AWS PrivateLink-style interface endpoints, and site-to-site VPN for this shape of deployment? Specifically: setup complexity, how source-ip/identity surfaces, failover options, and where we should default in a high-compliance environment.

If helpful, I can share a network diagram — I attached our very rough topology.

Cheers,
Maria

Hi Maria — good notes and thanks for the topology. High level first, then recommended fallback/playbook.

Quick summary:
- PrivateLink (interface endpoints): strong isolation (no cross-VPC routing of tenant traffic), simplest from a security posture standpoint because you can pin to endpoint policies and keep the Redwood dataplane behind an endpoint. Drawbacks: you generally lose original source IP unless you run a proxy or preserve source via X-Forwarded-For; theres also per-endpoint throughput and ENI limits to mind. Great default when you must avoid routing table expansion and want tight security controls.

- VPC Peering / cloud native peering: native L3 routing preservation of source IP (if both sides are in-cloud), very low latency and fewer hop penalties. Downsides: peering requires route table management and can increase blast radius; its best for high-throughput, low-latency dataplane connections within the same cloud region/account boundary. Not always possible if the customer wants strict separation or is multi-cloud.

- Site-to-Site VPN (IPsec/MPLS): operationally flexible and quickest to stand up in air-gapped or complex on-prem setups. Source IP preservation depends on your NAT design (if you don't SNAT, you'll preserve source; many customers SNAT at edge which breaks tenant visibility). VPNs can be higher latency and less predictable; for production SLOs we recommend a managed / redundant pair with BGP and monitoring.

Recommended fallback playbook (short):
1) Default: PrivateLink when isolation + compliance are primary requirements and throughput fits the endpoint profile. Add a small TCP-proxy (customer or Redwood-managed) in the customer VPC to capture original source IPs in X-Forwarded-For and to do per-tenant ACLing if needed.
2) If you need native source IP for policy enforcement and both sides are cloud-hosted: use VPC Peering and avoid SNAT between the control plane and hosts. Put a thin egress filter at the tenant boundary.
3) If you are on-prem or have limited public IPs and cannot create interface endpoints: use a site-to-site VPN as a pragmatic fallback. Run dual paths where possible: primary PrivateLink (or peering) with VPN as failover. Use healthchecks and a small policy engine in the VPC to prefer the primary.

Operational notes and gotchas:
- SNAT/Source IP: definitely call out for NetOps — if you SNAT at border you will need to introduce per-tenant mapping in the proxy or correlate logs at the firewall.
- Throttles & ENI limits (PrivateLink): plan for ENI and per-ENI throughput; if youre at high TPS we often advise a dedicated endpoint in the account with multiple ENIs and autoscale-friendly architecture.
- Inter-region / multi-cloud: PrivateLink is typically regional; peering likewise. For multi-region, use regional endpoints and cross-region replication or a failover VPN.
- Observability: ensure TLS client certs (mTLS) or per-API-key tagging so we can trace requests end-to-end across the fallback paths.

Attaching a short checklist and a diagram (privatedeploy-connector-checklist.pdf and onprem-fallback-diagram.png). Ill loop Ben and Karthik for runbook/operational items.

Thanks Kim — adding a few operational bullets from an infra perspective that Ive seen missed in pilots: 

- Healthcheck & failover glue: implement an active healthcheck with a small route preference (local preference with BGP or policy-based routing) so VPN only becomes active on dataplane failure. Dont rely purely on admin toggles.
- SNAT avoidance pattern: if you can, preserve source IP by moving SNAT to a NAT gateway that tags flows with a deterministic mapping and expose that mapping to your logging pipeline for correlation. If thats impossible, use the proxy approach Kim suggested.
- Certificate & endpoint rotation: if you use interface endpoints, automate cert rotation and endpoint policy changes with Terraform or CloudFormation to avoid manual ACL drift.
- Cost profile: PrivateLink has a per-Gb egress cost and per-hour ENI costs; peering is cheap but may require VPC cross-account setup costs; VPN costs depend on tunnel uptime and vendor. Budget for failover tunnels (redundant pairs).

Operational checklist snippet (for NetOps):
- Confirm static egress IP pool size + request additional if oversubscribed.
- Decide SNAT boundary and communicate to app teams.
- Deploy proxy or endpoint(s) in staging and exercise failover.

Happy to help run a tabletop with EdgeGate NetOps next week.

—Ben
